definition: United States v. Hemani, 608 U.S. (2026), is a U.S. Supreme Court case focused on the scope of the Second Amendment to the United States Constitution. In this case, Hemani was suspected of terrorism-related activities, and complied with a search of his home in 2022. During this process, the FBI found a handgun lawfully registered to Hemani, and he pointed agents to some marijuana that was on the property. Hemani was cooperative in the search, surrendered the handgun to authorities, and admitted to being a regular marijuana user in an interview with law enforcement. Hemani was subsequently charged under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits any person who is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substances listed in the 21 U.S.C. § 802 from possessing a firearm. In an opinion by Justice Gorsuch, the Supreme Court held that the law as applied to Hemani was a violation of the Second Amendment. During the course of litigation, the Supreme Court decided United States v. Rahimi, 602 U.S. 680 (2024), rejecting the Fifth Circuit's earlier challenge to 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which prohibits firearm possession by certain individuals subject to domestic-violence restraining orders. Hemani subsequently reached the Supreme Court as an as-applied challenge to § 922(g)(3). The issue presented to the Supreme Court in this case was whether the prosecution of Hemani under § 922(g)(3) infringed on the Second Amendment. The Court applied the Second Amendment framework set out in N.Y. State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022). The government conceded that § 922(g)(3) burdens conduct protected by the Second Amendment, thus the government had the burden to demonstrate that the statute as applied to Hemani was consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation. In order to meet this burden, the government relied on historical “habitual drunkard” laws and argued that they were relevantly similar to § 922(g)(3) in their purpose and operation.
